title: Aditya Birla Group Levies 0.25% Brand Royalty on Grasim and Hindalco, Caps Fee at ₹225 Crore
excerpt: The conglomerate formalizes a brand-usage fee across its flagship companies, triggering a nearly 2% stock drop in Hindalco and raising questions about promoter-level charges in Indian business groups.
body:
• Aditya Birla Group companies will pay a 0.25% royalty on revenue for using the group's brand name, capped at ₹225 crore annually per company.
  • Grasim Industries estimates its annual royalty payment at roughly ₹125 crore based on projected revenues, well within the cap.
  • Hindalco Industries will begin payments from fiscal year 2027, with its subsidiary Novelis also covered under the framework.
  • Hindalco led losses on the Nifty after the announcement, dropping nearly 2%, while UltraTech Cement and Grasim also declined.

A Formal Brand Fee Takes Shape

The Aditya Birla Group has introduced a structured brand royalty framework that will require its listed flagship companies — including Grasim Industries, Hindalco Industries, and Hindalco's U.S.-listed subsidiary Novelis — to pay 0.25% of their revenue for the use of the Aditya Birla brand name. The fee is capped at ₹225 crore per company per year.

Grasim Industries, the group's diversified conglomerate with interests spanning cement, chemicals, textiles, and paints, expects its annual royalty payment to be approximately ₹125 crore based on projected revenues. The company reported consolidated revenue of ₹48,716 crore in Q1 FY27, a 21% year-on-year jump, alongside its highest-ever quarterly EBITDA.

Hindalco Feels the Market Impact

Hindalco Industries, the group's metals and mining flagship and parent of Novelis, will begin paying the royalty from fiscal year 2027. Hindalco managing director Satish Pai described the framework as marking "a shift" in how the group formalizes the value of its brand across operating companies.

Markets reacted negatively to the announcement. Hindalco took the biggest hit on the Nifty, while UltraTech Cement and Grasim also dropped nearly 2%. Investors interpreted the royalty as an additional promoter-level charge that could compress margins, particularly for companies with large revenue bases where even a small percentage adds up to substantial outflows.

"The framework marks a shift in how the group formalizes the value of its brand across operating companies."

— Satish Pai, Managing Director, Hindalco Industries

The Brand Royalty Debate in India Inc.

Brand royalty payments from listed subsidiaries to promoter-held entities have been a recurring point of debate in Indian corporate governance. The Tata Group charges a similar brand fee, typically around 0.25% of revenue, from its listed companies. The Mahindra Group and Godrej Group have comparable arrangements.

Proponents argue the fee reflects genuine brand value — the Aditya Birla name carries recognition across 40 countries and lends credibility in capital markets, talent acquisition, and customer trust. Critics, particularly minority shareholders, view such fees as value extraction by promoter families that dilutes returns to public investors.

The ₹225 crore cap is designed to address scale concerns. For a company like Novelis, which reported over $17 billion in revenue for its most recent fiscal year and is preparing for a U.S. IPO, an uncapped percentage-based fee could have been significantly larger. The cap effectively limits the royalty to a fixed ceiling regardless of revenue growth.

Group Context and Scale

The Aditya Birla Group, led by chairman Kumar Mangalam Birla, operates across metals, cement, fashion, financial services, and telecom. Its combined market capitalization spans trillions of rupees, and its $20 billion investment pipeline includes capacity expansions across cement and downstream aluminium.

The brand fee formalization comes as the group pursues several high-profile moves: a consortium including Aditya Birla Group acquired the Royal Challengers Bengaluru cricket franchise for ₹16,600 crore earlier this year, and Novelis's planned U.S. listing is expected to be one of the largest IPOs by an Indian-group subsidiary.

What Investors Are Watching

The immediate stock market reaction suggests investors will monitor how the royalty interacts with each company's margin profile. Grasim, with its diversified revenue streams including the new Birla Opus paints business, can absorb the charge more easily than lower-margin businesses. For Hindalco, where aluminium is cyclical and margins can compress during downturns, the fixed-percentage nature of the fee adds a floor cost that doesn't flex with profitability.

Analysts expect the framework to be scrutinized during upcoming earnings calls, with questions likely around the governance process for setting and revising the rate, the specific entity receiving the royalty, and whether independent directors signed off on the arrangement.
